hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.hook: 'Here's how to sell AI to Main Street with no audience and no money, step by step.' 1,134 bookmarks on 527 likes: saved as a playbook.
hits.draft_en:
Greg's right that Main Street is the big AI opportunity. The pitch that gets you in the door isn't AI, though. It's "what happens to your business if this computer dies tonight?"

After nearly 30 years in disaster recovery, here's how I'd open that conversation:

1. Ask where the customer list, the books and the bookings actually live.
2. Ask when someone last restored any of it.
3. Offer to test one restore, free, on a spare machine.
4. Fix whatever breaks, then quote for the rest.

Trust first. The AI work comes after.
hits.video_tip: 45-60s talking head outside a local shop or café: hold up four fingers and count the steps off as you say them, with each step on screen. End on 'trust first' and hold for a beat.

hits.name: Tony Dinh
hits.hook: 'NEW APP!!!' launch that rides the security-incident wave: a macOS clipboard manager that hides API keys and secrets. 110 replies.
hits.draft_en:
Everyone's building tools to stop secrets leaking. Good.

Almost nobody is checking whether they can get their data back after something leaks anyway.

Patching keeps attackers out. Restores keep you in business. I'm building CrossRestore for the second job.
hits.video_tip: 20-30s face cam: say the first two lines, then cut to a screen recording of a restore running on a test machine. No client data on screen.

narrative_synthesis: AI money is today's meta: Greg's numbered Anthropic S-1 takeaways and levelsio's 'only Big AI wins' and $GOOGL posts pulled the biggest numbers. Step-by-step playbooks got saved far more than liked (Greg's Main Street guide), and Tony's secrets-hiding app shows the security-incident wave still sells launches. Contrast analogies (robotaxi vs farmer, painter vs doctor) carried dvassallo. Recovery is still the gap: lots of 'keep secrets safe', almost nobody asking 'can you get it back'.
